Backtest review · Gold

Fifteen years and one gold crash: an honest stress test of a gold trend strategy

Our gold strategy looked excellent on the data it was built on. We re-ran it, unchanged, on fifteen years of exchange data, including a 45% crash it had never seen. This is everything we found, good and bad.

November 2026 · about 15 minutes to read

The short version

  • It survived the crash. In 2011–2014, years it was never tuned on, gold lost 21% and the strategy made 4%, with a third of gold's drawdown.
  • Its headline Sharpe of 1.08 was flattered. On fifteen years of clean data it is 0.69, holding costs included. Gold's is 0.32.
  • Its strength is limiting losses, not predicting gold. Worst drawdown -19%, against -45% for gold. Its timing advantage over simply holding gold at the same risk is too small to be statistically meaningful.
  • Realistic expectation: about 7–10% a year at standard risk, a worst drawdown near 20%, and roughly three-year stretches below a previous high.

1. Why we re-tested it

Every trading strategy looks good on the data used to design it. Its settings are chosen because they worked on that data, so its backtest is partly a measure of how well it fits the past. The only honest test is data it has never seen.

Our gold strategy, which we call "the champion", had two weaknesses there:

  • Its headline Sharpe of about 1.08 came from 2015 onward. That is the same period we used to choose its settings, and gold mostly rose over it. A long-only strategy looks good in a bull market almost by default.
  • Our older long gold history was stitched together from two brokers' price feeds. That kind of splice had already produced two fake results in our research, so we couldn't trust it for this.

An earlier test ran a daily-bar version back to 2002 and suggested the strategy survived the 2011–2015 crash. But the live strategy runs on 4-hour bars, and clean 4-hour gold data before 2015 wasn't available. So the question stayed open: is the 4-hour strategy genuinely good, or did it look good because of when we tested it?

2. How the strategy works

It's deliberately simple, and every rule is fixed in advance:

Long only

It buys gold or holds a small amount. It never bets on gold falling. Across our research, the short side of gold lost money in every family of signals we tried. Gold's long-run upward drift makes selling it a losing habit.

Two trend signals, combined

  • Trend: compares fast and slow moving averages of price at three speeds, from about 16 to 256 trading days. The further the fast averages sit above the slow ones, the stronger the trend.
  • Breakout: measures where today's price sits within its recent range over 10, 20 and 40 days. Near the top of the range scores high.

The two are combined into a forecast between 0 and 2. Strong signals are boosted and weak ones shrunk (the score is raised to the power 1.5), so the strategy commits when trends are clear and stays light when they're not.

A small resting position

Even with no trend, the forecast doesn't drop below about 0.15. It keeps a token long position, so it's never fully out when a new uptrend starts.

Sizing by volatility

The position is sized so the account's risk stays near a 10% yearly volatility target. When gold becomes jumpy, it holds less; when gold is calm, it holds more. Over fifteen years the position averaged 0.65× the account (median 0.44×), and only 5% of the time was it above 1.8×.

Checked every 4 hours, traded only when needed

It recalculates every 4 hours, but only trades when the target position has moved meaningfully away from what it holds. That keeps costs down.

3. The data, and how we checked it

We used hourly CME gold futures bars from June 2010 to November 2026, from Databento. It's one source, the exchange where gold's price is actually set. Futures contracts expire every few months, so we stitched consecutive contracts together and removed the artificial price jump at each switch.

Before trusting it, we checked it against the gold our live strategy actually trades at a broker:

  • Hour by hour, the two prices move together with a correlation of 0.986. One hour apart, the correlation is about zero, so the timestamps line up.
  • On the years both cover (2017 onward), the strategy's daily results on the two data sources correlate at 0.95.

One difference matters. A futures price already includes the cost of holding gold, which is roughly the interest rate. A broker charges that cost separately, as overnight swap. So these results include the cost of holding, and on recent years, when interest rates were high, they come out lower than our broker-data backtest (Sharpe 0.86 against 1.12 for 2017 onward).

The test starts in June 2011, because the slowest trend signal needs about a year of history before it can trade. Every comparison below starts on the same date.

4. The out-of-sample test: 2011 to 2014

The strategy's settings were chosen on data from 2015 onward, so everything before 2015 is a genuine out-of-sample test. It's also the worst stretch for gold in a generation.

Jun 2011 – Dec 2014ReturnSharpeWorst drawdown
Champion+4.4%+0.18−15.5%
Always long, same risk−13.1%−0.34−28.0%
Gold buy & hold−21.4%−0.24−40.9%

Gold lost a fifth of its value and the strategy made a small profit, with a drawdown well under half of gold's. A 0.18 Sharpe is nothing to celebrate on its own. What matters is that the strategy held its ground while everything that simply owned gold got hurt.

5. Inside the crash

How did it avoid the damage? It didn't predict the crash. It noticed the uptrend had stopped and stayed small:

52%of 4-hour checks in 2011–15 spent at the small resting position
0.56average forecast in the bear market (scale 0–2)
0.40×average position in the bear, against 0.76× from 2016 on

It didn't need to know the crash was coming. It only needed to notice the uptrend had stopped, and then stay small.

Notice the trade-off in the chart. Every failed rally cost something, which is why the strategy still lost about 6% across the full bear (Sep 2011 – Dec 2015). Always-long at the same risk lost 22%, and gold lost 42%.

Three things stand out:

  • Fewer than half its months are positive (44%), yet it more than doubles the always-long return. That's what trend following looks like: many small losses, a few large gains. Its best month (+15.9%) is nearly three times the size of its worst (-5.9%), and its returns lean strongly to the upside (skewness +1.4).
  • Its drawdowns are far shallower than gold's, and it recovers faster: its longest stretch below a previous high was 3.3 years, against 13.7 years for gold.
  • It runs slightly above its 10% volatility target (12.3%), because its strongest signals size up to twice the base position.

The strategy was positive in 81% of years and beat gold in 69% of them. Its worst calendar year was 2013 (−7.3%), when gold fell 28%. It lags badly in a straight-up boom, as in 2025, when gold rose 56% and the strategy made 23%, because it keeps its risk constant rather than chasing the move.

8. Is it skill or luck?

Fifteen years sounds like a lot, but for a strategy that trades long trends it holds only a handful of independent episodes. So we asked how confident we can be, using a bootstrap: resampling the daily returns in monthly blocks thousands of times.

  • The strategy's Sharpe ratio lies between 0.18 and 1.19 with 95% confidence. It's clearly above zero, but the range is wide.
  • Against gold buy-and-hold: the strategy's Sharpe is higher in about 94% of resamples. That's strong evidence of a better risk-adjusted return than simply owning gold.
  • Against always-long at the same risk: higher in only about 85% of resamples. That's suggestive, not proof. A good part of the improvement over gold comes from sizing by volatility rather than from timing.

Our honest reading: the strategy reliably turns gold into a smoother investment, with similar or better returns and much smaller crashes. Whether its trend timing adds much beyond that can't be proven from fifteen years of data.

9. Costs

A strategy that only works with near-zero costs is fragile. This one trades rarely, turning over about 28× its account value a year, so costs barely matter:

Cost per tradeSharpe
0 bp0.70
1 bp0.69
2 bp0.68
3 bp0.67
5 bp0.64
10 bp0.58

Ten times our baseline cost lowers the Sharpe from 0.69 to 0.58. Costs aren't what decides this strategy; holding costs (swap) matter more. A swap-free account would add back roughly the interest rate a year on the gold held.

10. What didn't help

We've spent months trying to improve this strategy. Almost nothing beat the simple version once compared fairly, meaning at the same risk level and against random-timing benchmarks:

  • Market-regime filters (trading only when trend strength or volatility looks favourable) cut returns and made drawdowns worse.
  • Short selling lost money in every form.
  • Adding more trend assets diluted the result. Gold plus bitcoin was the best pair we found.
  • Volume and order-flow signals ("footprint" charts built from real buy and sell volume) added nothing once price was accounted for.
  • Machine-learning timing (gradient boosting, LSTMs, a transformer trained on candles) didn't beat random entry timing.
  • Taking profits early or scaling out raised the win rate but lowered total returns. Trend followers make their money on the trades they let run.

The one lever that clearly worked was lowering the cost of holding: swap-free gold accounts improved results more than any signal tweak.

11. What to expect if you run it

  • Returns: about 7–10% a year at a 10% volatility target, before broker swap. Scale the target up or down to change both return and drawdown proportionally.
  • Drawdowns: expect a peak-to-trough fall of around 15–20% at some point, and several years with small losses.
  • Patience: twice in fifteen years it spent about three years below a previous high: October 2012 to February 2016, and August 2020 to March 2024.
  • Underperformance in booms: in a year like 2025, simply holding gold will beat it by a wide margin. That's the price of insurance against a year like 2013.
  • Don't intervene. Most of the return comes from a few long trends. Closing positions early to "bank" gains removes exactly those.

12. FAQ

Why compare against "always long at the same risk"?

Because the strategy changes two things at once: when it holds gold (timing) and how much (volatility sizing). Holding a constant long position with the same volatility sizing isolates the timing. Beating gold is easy if you only control risk; beating the constant-long version shows the timing itself helps.

Why 4-hour bars?

The live strategy runs on them. A daily-bar version tested back to 2002 gave a similar full-period Sharpe (0.64) and the same crash protection, so the result isn't specific to the bar size.

Isn't fifteen years enough to prove it?

For trend following, not quite. The strategy's returns come from a small number of multi-month trends, so fifteen years holds perhaps a dozen independent bets. That's why the confidence interval on the Sharpe is so wide.

Would it have worked before 2010?

The daily version, tested 2002–2026, kept the same character: similar returns to holding gold at the same risk, with roughly half the drawdown. It lost 11% in the 2011–15 bear while gold lost 42%.

Why not also bet on gold falling?

We tested it extensively. Shorting gold lost money in every signal family over the long run, because gold drifts upward over time and short positions pay the holding cost the other way. Long-only roughly doubled the Sharpe of the long/short versions.

Method. Data: CME Globex gold futures (GC, most-active contract by volume), hourly bars via Databento, June 2010 – November 2026, back-adjusted at contract rolls, grouped into 4-hour bars on the broker server clock (New York + 7h). Strategy: long-only blend of an EWMAC trend forecast (16/64, 32/128, 64/256 days) and a breakout forecast (10, 20, 40 days), concentrated with exponent 1.5, floor 0.15, cap 2. Sizing: 10% annual volatility target, exponentially weighted volatility (half-life 42 bars), 10% no-trade buffer. Costs 1 basis point per trade (sweep shown above). Futures returns already include holding costs. Confidence intervals: moving-block bootstrap, 21-day blocks, 2,000 resamples. Full working paper and code available on request.

Disclaimer. This is a backtest: past simulated results, not live trading and not investment advice. Real trading adds slippage, broker costs and execution risk. Past performance does not guarantee future results.
